query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Minor alloying of NbMoTaW with approximately 5 at% Zr will improve its room-temperature ductility by enhancing dislocation mobility while preserving the alloy’s high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Introduce roughly 5 at% Zr into the NbMoTaW system via controlled alloying (e.g., arc-melting or sputtering) to ensure homogeneous distribution
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature, high-temperature mechanical assessments at 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments using sequential Kr and He ion irradiations under controlled fluence conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and modified defect/dislocation interactions induced by the Zr atoms
generation.mechanism: The addition of Zr is expected to create localized lattice softening that lowers the stress needed for dislocation movement at room temperature without significantly altering the intrinsic BCC structure. This minor compositional tweak maintains the high-temperature phase stability and limits the growth of irradiation-induced defect clusters by retaining a high density of trapping sites similar to the baseline alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: At room temperature, the Zr-modified NbMoTaW is predicted to exhibit increased ductility (higher elongation and lower yield stress for plastic deformation) relative to the untreated alloy; at 1600 °C, the high-temperature strength and overall phase integrity should remain comparable; and under irradiation, the alloy is expected to demonstrate similar resistance to defect accumulation and hardening as the baseline NbMoTaW.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be valid for minor additions (up to approximately 5 at% Zr). Excessive Zr content might disrupt the refractory properties or the single-phase BCC structure and could compromise high-temperature performance or irradiation tolerance.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative improvements in room-temperature ductility and preserved high-temperature/irradiation properties are anticipated, the precise quantitative changes in dislocation mobility and defect interaction require experimental validation. Optimal Zr content and distribution effects remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy and one of NbMoTaW alloyed with 5 at% Zr. Ensure homogeneous distribution of elements via appropriate processing methods (e.g., arc-melting or sputtering). Perform tensile tests at room temperature to quantify elongation and yield strength, high-temperature tests at 1600 °C to assess strength and phase stability, and irradiation tests using controlled Kr and He ion beams to simulate radiation damage. Microstructural analysis (using TEM, XRD, etc.) should be conducted post-irradiation to compare defect densities and bubble formation.
measurements: Irradiation-induced microstructure (defect cluster size and density via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-modified NbMoTaW alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility while either showing reduced high-temperature mechanical performance or altered irradiation response (e.g., increased defect clustering or hardening) compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Crystal distortion is caused by the microstrain, which is stimulated by the stresses and defect formation under irradiation. Most similar research was concerned with microstrain and lattice parameter changes in HEAs. In HEAs and steels including 316L and 304H, helium irradiation usually leads to lattice expansion [,]. Helium irradiation led to lattice expansion in VCrFeMn []. However, in HEAs such as non-equiatomic Ti2ZrHfV0.5Mo0.2, lattice parameters can be reduced by helium ion irradiation due to higher lattice distortion []. Lattice expansion and microstrain can also be increased by irradiation with non-heavy ions such as Ni and C. Irradiation by Ni ions resulted in lattice expansion in FeCoNiCr and FeCoNiCrMn []. Irradiation of (WTiVNbTa)C5 high-entropy ceramics by carbon ions at higher fluences led to higher microstrain and lattice expansion at room temperature, while higher temperature irradiation led to a lower microstrain []. The maximum He bubble size in Hf1Ta HEA can reach more than 16 nm with average sizes of 10.5 and 13.7 nm at different fluences, which was conducive to enhancing the interaction between He bubbles and dislocations and improving the hardness. Thus, the formation of large He bubbles in the irradiated Hf1Ta HEA could be considered as the main cause of hardening. Compared with the sample irradiated at low fluence, the larger and denser He bubbles generated in the sample irradiated at high fluence can interact with the dislocations more effectively, which led to the higher hardness increment and hardening fraction in the Hf1Ta HEA irradiated at the fluence of 3 × 1016 ions/cm2. Additionally, Zhao [] and Shi [] proposed that residual density of vacancies and interstitials produced by irradiation could be greatly reduced by the effective recombination in the HEAs. cited_evidence.text: A larger number of large blisters in Ni can be due to more damage produced than in HEAs as estimated by SRIM, which increases the portion of helium-vacancy clusters, leads to the accumulation of He bubbles and facilitates their growth. Observation of blisters in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA could be due to the damage from Kr irradiation supplying vacancies for He bubble formation [] and thus contributing to blistering. Presence of smaller blisters or their lack in the HEAs is probably related to their lattice distortion and the lower mobility of point defects, which affect the bubble nucleation and growth [], but no surface exfoliation was observed. A study of the TaTiNbZr HEA irradiated by high-flux He ions at 0–70 eV showed that blister size increases with the increasing energy of ions, and one of the reasons why blisters and microcracks form is the oversaturation of helium and accumulation of He bubbles under the surface []. Figure 6 presents the phases of Ni and HEAs after irradiation by krypton ions and sequential irradiation by krypton and helium ions. Sequential irradiation with Kr and He ions led to a change from tensile to compressive stresses in the HEAs in both Regions I and II compared to unirradiated states. But in Region I, stress in Ni remained tensile, while compressive stresses of −54 MPa and −258 MPa formed in CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi, respectively. In Region II, compressive macrostresses reached larger values of −131.5 MPa, −300 MPa and −613.5 MPa in Ni, CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi, respectively. The trend of compressive stress formation similar to He-only irradiation could be due to increased damage and helium bubbles accumulation in the HEAs. Irradiation by Kr ions led to a decrease in the dislocation density by 1.6–2.3 times in Regions I and II and sequential irradiation with Kr and He ions to an increase of dislocation densities in Region II by 11–15 times for CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeMnNi, respectively. Most notable macrostress and dislocation density changes were observed in the peak helium implantation region. After irradiation, the CoCrFeMnNi HEA was characterized by higher macrostresses and dislocation density compared to CoCrFeNi.

The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles. reading.lever: Minorly alloy NbMoTaW with a ductilizing element (e.g., Ti or Zr) to enhance dislocation mobility while preserving high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
reading.why: Prior evidence in Zr–Nb–Ti MEAs demonstrates that compositional tweaks can yield improved room-temperature ductility and robust irradiation resistance, a strategy not yet applied to NbMoTaW.
